headline: An unsigned purge anchor could erase the audit trail and be reported as intact, and a CSRF exemption turned on a header the attacker writes
summary:
The audit chain records where a retention purge legitimately removed rows, so verification can tell an accounted-for gap from a deletion. That record carried no signature, sat in no chain and was covered by no checkpoint, while verification validated only its shape and then adopted its hash as the chain origin — discarding every row at or below the counter it named. Three SQL statements erased a trail and the volume still verified clean. It is a cheaper attack than the relink-and-forge one the chain already refuses, which is what makes it a bypass rather than a partial defence. The anchor is now signed and checked before any gap is honoured.

`csrfProtect`'s `skipStateless` waived the token check for a request carrying an `Authorization` header. Presence is not authenticity: an attacker composing a cross-site request writes their own headers. Worse, the header says nothing about which credential authenticated the request, and `attachUser` with `tokenFrom: "both"` reads the cookie first — so a request carrying both was authenticated by exactly the ambient credential the gate protects, and skipped the gate on a header nobody read. The exemption now turns on the absence of a cookie, and it no longer waives the origin check.

Also: a certificate renewal reached four mail listeners and not the fifth, a hosted-domain set could not change without a restart, and a checkpoint read the chain tip outside the lock that makes appends atomic.

items.title: The audit purge anchor is signed, and an unsigned one no longer excuses a gap (#674)
items.body:
`_blamejs_audit_purge_anchor` records where a retention purge removed rows, so verification can distinguish an accounted-for gap from a deletion. Verification validated that its hash was 128 hex characters and its counter a finite number, then adopted that hash as the chain origin and discarded every row at or below that counter.

So the record that says "everything below here was legitimately removed" was the one thing in the system writable without a key. Delete the rows, delete the checkpoints covering them, insert one anchor naming any hash and counter, and the trail is gone while verification reports the volume intact. That is less work than the relink-and-forge attack the chain already refuses and it erases more, so it was not a weaker version of the defence — it was a way around it.

The anchor now carries a signature and the fingerprint of the key that made it, over its counter, its adopted hash, the archive it names and when it was written. Change any of those and the signature stops matching. Verification checks it before honouring anything: an anchor with no signature, one whose signature does not verify, or one naming a key the volume has no record of is refused with a reason, and the rows below it are NOT treated as purged.

The archive itself is still not resolved — nothing in the framework knows where a consumer keeps bundles — so verification no longer implies that it was. A honoured gap is reported as a signed counter that was believed, with the archive named but unverified, and `blamejs audit verify-chain` says so on its own line. Asserting a verified archive was the part that cost nothing to fix and made the difference between a weak guarantee and a false one.

Checking that signature needs the audit-signing public key, and not every verifier has one loaded: `blamejs audit verify-chain` opens a database file directly and never initializes signing. It takes `--audit-key <path>` for the PEM, and `b.auditChain.verifyChain` takes `opts.resolvePublicKey` for the same purpose in-process. Without either, a signed anchor is reported as UNCHECKED rather than as invalid — a purged volume is not a tampered one, and an operator has to be able to tell those apart. `verify-chain` exits 3 in that case, distinct from the 1 it exits on a chain that failed, and the result carries `purgeAnchorUnchecked` for a caller doing the same in-process. `b.auditChain.purgeAnchorPayload` builds the exact bytes the signature covers, so an anchor can be checked out of band against an archived copy.

The anchor table gains two columns for this. A local volume adds them on the next open. An external Postgres, MySQL or SQLite backend gets them from `b.frameworkSchema.ensureSchema()`, which now issues an idempotent `ADD COLUMN` for each — a table that already exists is untouched by `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, so re-running setup was not enough on its own. A purge checks it can record a signature BEFORE deleting anything, and refuses with `audit-tools/anchor-not-signable` if it cannot: the rows stay, and the operator is told what to fix.

Audit signing is now initialized before the boot chain verification that needs it, so a previously purged volume can check its own anchor as it starts. A deployment running `auditSigning: false` has no key and never will — it has no checkpoints either, having opted out of signature-based tamper evidence — so its anchor is adopted as before and the verification result records that the gap was trusted rather than verified, with `signatureVerified: false`. Refusing to boot there would punish an operator for declining a protection they never had.

**Upgrading.** A volume purged by an earlier version has an anchor with no signature. It is no longer honoured, so verification reports the gap rather than skipping it. Re-running the purge against the retained archive writes a signed anchor; until then the rows below it are treated as missing rather than as archived, which is the honest reading of a record that cannot prove where it came from.

items.title: `csrfProtect` `skipStateless` turns on the absence of a cookie, not on a header (#663)
items.body:
The exemption exists because a request with no ambient credential cannot be forged on a victim's behalf: CSRF spends a cookie the browser attaches by itself. It tested for an `Authorization` header as well.

Presence is not authenticity. An attacker composing a cross-site request writes their own headers, so `Authorization: Bearer nonsense` met the condition by being typed. And the header says nothing about which credential authenticated the request: `b.middleware.attachUser` with `tokenFrom: "both"` reads the cookie FIRST, so a request carrying a session cookie and a junk bearer header was authenticated by exactly the ambient credential the gate protects, and skipped the gate because of a header nothing had read. The two middlewares disagreed about which credential was in play, and the disagreement is what opened it.

The test is now the absence of a Cookie header, and nothing else. A bearer client that also sends an unrelated cookie is validated like any other request; deciding otherwise needs the auth layer's verdict about which credential authenticated it, which header presence cannot supply.

The exemption also sits below the origin cross-check now instead of above it, so `checkOrigin` is no longer waived by it. A consumer that asked for an origin check asked for something the token compare does not provide, and there is no reading of "stateless" under which a cross-origin state change becomes acceptable.

**Upgrading.** A caller relying on the header to skip the token check now needs to send the token, or to send no cookie. This is the shape the option was documented to cover; the header was never evidence of anything.

items.title: A checkpoint reads the chain tip under the lock that makes appends atomic (#673)
items.body:
A checkpoint is a signed statement about a specific tip, and the value of that signature is that the pair it names was real. The tip read that feeds one ran outside the mutex the chain writer holds across its own read-tip → insert, so it could land in the middle of an append and pair a counter with a hash that were never the tip together. The signature over that pair is valid, the arithmetic is self-consistent, and it describes a state the chain was never in.

The read now takes the same lock. It is held for the read only: signing is post-quantum and slow, every concurrent append queues behind that lock, and holding it across the signature would charge that cost to unrelated writers without adding a guarantee — a checkpoint claims a prefix, not that nothing has been appended since.

A second, unreachable insert path into `audit_log` is removed. It took no lock and computed no row hash, and a future reader finding two insert paths into the chain table would reasonably have assumed both were live.

items.title: A certificate renewal reaches the ManageSieve listener (#671)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.mx`, `.submission`, `.imap` and `.pop3` read `opts.tlsContext` at the point they need a context, so a consumer supplying an accessor gets the renewed certificate on the next connection. `.managesieve` captured it at construction, calling that accessor exactly once and serving the boot certificate for the life of the process.

Certificates renew every 60 to 90 days on any automated CA, so the frozen one expires while every piece of surrounding evidence says rotation is working: the watcher fired, the context rebuilt, and it simply never reached this one listener. That is worse than a listener that never supported rotation, because nothing reports it.

It now reads the option per connection like its siblings.

The rotation example in `b.mail.server.tls.context` was also wrong. It showed `mx.replaceTlsContext(newCtx)`, a method no listener implements and none needs: pass `get tlsContext() { return tls.secureContext; }` and a reload reaches the next connection with nothing to swap. Passing `tlsContext: tls.secureContext` copies the context current at boot, which is the frozen form.

items.title: The hosted-domain set can change while the server runs (#661)
items.body:
`b.mail.server.mx.create` captured `localDomains` at construction, so the answer to "do we host this domain" was frozen at boot. Hosting a domain is administrative state, not configuration — operators add and withdraw them while the process runs.

Withdrawing is the case that bit: the operator disables a domain, every management surface agrees it is gone, and the listener keeps answering 250 at RCPT for it until a restart, with nothing signalling that mail is still arriving. Adding is milder but still wrong — a new domain draws 550 5.7.1, which a sending queue reads as permanent and drops rather than retrying.

`localDomains` now also accepts a function, answered per recipient. The neighbouring `recipientPolicy` already was, which is what made the frozen half odd: two parts of one question answered a line apart with different currency. The array form is unchanged and still validated once at boot.

An entry a live set returns that `b.guardDomain` refuses is dropped, with an audit event naming it, rather than thrown on — this is the request path, and a throw there turns a typo in an admin form into a mail outage. Mail for that entry is refused; the rest of the set keeps serving. A set that cannot be read at all refuses every recipient.

`authservId` follows the same set rather than pinning to whichever domain was first at boot.
